claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.

A surrogate combining reduced-order high-fidelity micromechanical simulations with a transfer-learned deep-learning ensemble can predict the mechanical properties of hierarchical heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The deep-learning ensemble can be effectively pretrained using datasets from related high-entropy alloys.
Physics-based constraints and transfer learning can inform the surrogate-model architecture.
Hierarchical heterostructural features and chemical fluctuations mediate stress distribution in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical heterostructural features and chemical fluctuations mediate crack propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Encoding microstructural heterogeneities and chemical-fluctuation length scales allows the model to capture their effects on elastic and inelastic deformation.
Embedding physical constraints in a transfer-learned surrogate enables prior high-fidelity simulation data to be used to predict mechanical behavior.
Learning correlations between microstructural descriptors and mechanical properties reduces the need for full-scale computational sampling.
The surrogate will predict Young's modulus within approximately 10% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate will predict yield strength within approximately 10% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate will predict fracture toughness within approximately 15% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate will reduce computational time by roughly 90%, or at least one order of magnitude, relative to conventional simulation approaches.
Current approaches combining CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine learning have high computational cost.
Current computational approaches have limited reliability for predicting fracture toughness.
The model may lose reliability when target microstructural descriptors lie outside the training-data range.
The model may lose reliability under loading or temperature regimes absent from model development.
Fracture toughness is more difficult to model because crack propagation is complex.
Transfer-learning performance depends on similarity between the pretraining datasets and the target material's structural features.
